catalog_quote: The stressable element in Saliba is the syllable, not a single mora in a syllable. Stressed syllables are perceptually more prominent by greater duration and/or intensity, and/or higher pitch. Instrumental analysis shows that these three factors do not always coincide. There are different stress assignment constraints for verbs and nouns, and some of the other word classes are never stressed. For verbs, in at least 80% of the cases the stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, but heavy syllables tend to attract the primary stress. For nouns with lexical roots of three or more light syllables, about 70% of them have stress falling on the first syllable, and about 30% on the penultimate syllable. In lexical stems without suffixes, usually every second syllable preceding the primary stress receives secondary stress. This tendency is true for nouns, verbs, and adjectives. Gramm…

new_statements.rule_in_words: No phonemic tone or length; stress is non-contrastive. Default primary stress is penultimate (verbs >=80%, possessives used as nouns, and per Margetts 1999:11 'generally' for all words), with heavy (CVV/CVN) syllables tending to attract stress; but nouns whose roots have three or more light syllables mostly (~70%) take initial stress instead (e.g. 'Saliba, Margetts' named exception), the rest penultimate. Stress-shifting suffixes (object suffixes, -ma/-wa, perfect -ko) move primary stress to the new penult; subject prefixes, reduplication and enclitic determiners do not count.
new_statements.secondary_stress: OPD: in unsuffixed stems every second syllable preceding the primary stress gets secondary stress (nouns, verbs, adjectives); reduplicants may carry it; suffixes pull primary but not secondary stress rightward, so up to three syllables may separate them. Margetts 1999:11: in words of more than two syllables the initial syllable carries secondary stress (Oetzel 2019:6 says the same for words of more than four syllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Nouns with 3+ light-syllable roots ~70% initial-stressed (OPD); Margetts 1999:11 treats initial stress (e.g. the name Saliba) as unexplained lexical exceptions to penult. Heavy syllables attract stress in verbs. Object suffix -gomiu '2PL' always stressed on its first syllable. Determiners ta/ne/wa and adnominal possessives (kana, yodi) unstressed; subject agreement prefixes never stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on the phonological word = stem plus stress-affecting suffixes (Margetts uses stress shift as the suffix-vs-clitic diagnostic); enclitics outside the domain. OPD figures come from instrumental analysis of the Sawasawaga dialect; in connected speech only stressed syllables of clause-central words are lengthened (~2x).
new_statements.identity_note: All three sources describe Saliba proper (sali1295, ISO sbe); the OPD's prosodic observations are explicitly from the Sawasawaga dialect (Sariba Island), Margetts' data mainly from the Sidudu/Sawasawaga area. Not to be confused with Sáliba of Colombia/Venezuela (sali1298), whose SIL 'Fonologia Saliba' file also surfaces in the same SIL file store.

sources.note: pp. 3-4 'Suprasegmentals > Stress': no phonemic tone or length; stressable unit is the syllable; verbs: >=80% penultimate, heavy syllables attract primary stress; nouns with roots of 3+ light syllables: ~70% initial, ~30% penultimate; secondary stress on every second syllable before the primary in unsuffixed stems; subject prefixes/reduplication do not affect stress; suffixes pull primary stress rightward; -gomiu '2PL.OBJ' always stressed on its first syllable; determiners and adnominal possessives unstressed, possessives used alone get penultimate stress.

sources.note: Sec. 2.1 p. 11 (PDF p. 29; scan, scanned saved): 'Stress is not phonemic. Primary stress lies generally on the penultimate syllable. There are a few exceptions to this, like the name [Saliba] itself which carries primary stress on the first syllable.. In words with more than two syllables, the initial syllable carries secondary stress.' Suffixes (pronominal, -ma/-wa directionals, perfect -ko) can shift stress to the new penult; clitics (-wa, -ne determiners) do not (p. 11-12). Defers to Oetzel & Oetzel (1997) for a fuller phonological sketch.
